processing: A very early bush cultivar, most often made into flat green tea by Long Jing methods; the same leaf can also be made in other green styles and into black tea.
harvest_season: Exceptionally early: picking in Wenzhou begins in February, with sprouting around the start of spring and wider harvest by early March.
appearance_dry: Flat, smooth green blades much like West Lake Long Jing when made in that style, from plump, large buds.
appearance_wet: Plump, thick green buds and young leaves.
taste_profile: Wenzhou early teas are praised as tender, fresh and sweet; expect a light and clean cup rather than a deep one.

brewing.notes: Brew it like a Long Jing with slightly cooler water. These early shoots are fresh but gentle, so do not overdo the leaf.

vintage_note: Sold strictly as the current year's first flush, and the point of it is being first: the opening lots in February carry very high prices that fall quickly as the harvest widens. In 2026 the first picks from the Yongjia core area sold at around 2,800 yuan per jin. Drink it within months.
description:
Wuniuzao, 'Wuniu early', is both a cultivar and a tea. The bush comes from Yongjia county in Wenzhou, selected from a local plant by tea farmers, and its one great trick is timing: it sprouts around the start of spring, weeks before the classic Zhejiang teas.

That is why it has spread well beyond Yongjia, under the registered cultivar name Jiaming 1, and why it opens the green tea season across Zhejiang. It is a bush with medium, plump buds, and most of it is finished by Long Jing methods, so it looks very like West Lake tea.

The cup is typically tender, fresh and sweet, with less depth than later high-grown tea. Brew it as you would Long Jing, with water near 80 degrees and a short first steep.

The resemblance is the buying trap. Because it reaches market early and looks like Long Jing, it can be passed off as early West Lake tea. A very early 'Long Jing' from February deserves the question: is this Wuniuzao? Honestly labelled, it is a good tea and a real first taste of spring.
history:
The cultivar is attributed to farmers' single-plant selection in Luoxi township, Yongjia. Older local tradition says it was once lost and rediscovered roughly two hundred years ago; that account is thinly supported.

In modern times it became known under the name Jiaming 1 and was planted widely; research around 2008 reported it doing well as far north as southern Jiangsu. Yongjia Wuniuzao is one of the county teas under the Wenzhou Early Tea geographical indication, granted in 2020, and each year its harvest is treated as Zhejiang's opening of spring tea.
